papers.title: Integrative Medicine Approaches for Menopause.
papers.abstract: Women transitioning through menopause are often affected by vasomotor symptoms (VMS), bone loss, metabolic dysfunction, and increased cardiovascular risk. Although menopausal hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for menopause, nonhormonal strategies are essential for women with contraindications, personal preference, or a history of hormone-sensitive cancers. This narrative review evaluates evidence-based integrative approaches to menopause care, including lifestyle interventions, mind-body therapies, nutritional strategies, botanicals, and complementary modalities. Cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis have been shown to significantly reduce vasomotor symptom distress and are recommended as nonhormonal options. Although mindfulness-based interventions may improve sleep and quality of life (QOL), they are not recommended for the relief of VMS. Regular physical activity and dietary optimization are foundational for bone health and improving metabolic risk factors. Acupuncture may provide subjective improvements in overall symptom burden and QOL for some individuals. Despite the common use of phytoestrogens and various botanical therapies, high-quality evidence supporting their efficacy for VMS remains inconsistent. Consequently, these modalities are not advised for routine symptom management, particularly given their lack of standardization and potential safety concerns. Integrative approaches should be incorporated as part of an individualized, patient-centered care plan. Further research is needed to clarify effectiveness, safety, and optimal integration of these treatment approaches into clinical practice.

papers.title: Combined effects of hatha yoga and astaxanthin on depression, quality of life, and oxidative stress in postmenopausal women: A randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Menopause is associated with oestrogen deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and depressive symptoms, yet effective non-pharmacological interventions remain limited. This randomized controlled trial investigated the independent and combined effects of Hatha yoga and astaxanthin supplementation on psychological status, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial-related signaling in postmenopausal women. METHODS: One hundred sedentary postmenopausal women aged 55-60 years with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms were randomly assigned to four groups for 12 weeks: control (CG), Hatha yoga (HYG; 75 min/session, three sessions weekly), astaxanthin supplementation (ASG; 12 mg/day), or combined Hatha yoga plus astaxanthin (HYASG). The Hatha yoga program included āsana, prāṇāyāma, relaxation, and brief meditation. Outcomes included Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D), Menopause Rating Scale (MRS), Menopause-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (MENQOL), serum oxidative stress biomarkers (TAC, SOD, CAT, MDA, and TBARS), and peripheral blood expression of SIRT1, PGC-1α, and NRF1 assessed by qRT-PCR. RESULTS: Significant group × time interactions were observed for all major outcomes (p < 0.001). HYASG demonstrated the greatest improvements, with HAM-D scores decreasing by 45.1%, compared with 28.5% in HYG and 10.9% in ASG. In HYASG, MRS and MENQOL scores decreased by 41.1% and 50.0%, respectively. Combined intervention also produced the largest increases in TAC, SOD, and CAT activities and the greatest reductions in MDA and TBARS concentrations. SIRT1 and PGC-1α expression increased significantly in both yoga-containing groups, whereas NRF1 upregulation was most pronounced in HYASG. CONCLUSIONS: The combined intervention was associated with greater improvements in depressive symptoms, menopause-related outcomes, serum oxidative-stress biomarkers, and peripheral-blood mitochondrial-related gene expression than either intervention alone.

papers.title: Acute Effects of Brief Mindfulness Inductions on Executive Function Performance: A Systematic Review and Three-Level Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Evidence regarding the acute effect of brief mindfulness exercises (mindfulness inductions) on cognitive performance and executive functions (EFs) is mixed. This meta-analysis aimed to estimate the overall effect on the component of EFs (i.e. inhibitory control, working memory and cognitive flexibility) and investigate if the level of induced state of mindfulness explains this effect. The current pre-registered, three-level meta-analysis and systematic review included 66 published studies with 187 effect sizes, including a total of 2,503 participants in the experimental groups and 2,511 participants in control groups. Standardized mean differences were calculated for the post-test difference between the mindfulness and the control condition. Results from three-level meta-analytic model revealed that there is a small but significant effect of mindfulness inductions on overall EFs (k = 66, g = 0.09 95% CI [0.03, 0.16], p < 0.01). Moderator analyses did not indicate significant differences across EF components (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility); descriptive subgroup analyses yielded larger pooled estimates for inhibitory control than for cognitive flexibility and working memory. No evidence that the level of induced state mindfulness predicts effect sizes. It should be noted that moderator analysis might have been underpowered so these non-significant results should be interpreted with caution. Brief mindfulness exercises do not seem to improve overall EFs substantially. We conclude that the practical relevance of these null to small effect sizes is very limited.

papers.title: Eco-Affective Health: Exploring Emotions, Behavior and Well-Being in Sustainability.
papers.abstract: Sustainability transitions ultimately depend on sustained human engagement, yet sustainability science has largely overlooked a foundational determinant of whether such engagement endures: affect. Although emotions shape how environmental change is perceived, evaluated, and acted upon, they remain conceptually fragmented-typically treated as secondary outcomes, communication tools, or clinical concerns rather than as a core dimension of sustainability itself. This Perspective introduces Eco-Affective Health, offered as a conceptual lens rather than an exhaustive theory of environmental behavior that positions affective dynamics as a central regulatory mechanism operating in continuous interaction with cognitive appraisal and linking environmental conditions to human well-being, behavior, and the long-term viability of sustainability transitions. Eco-Affective Health conceptualizes emotions as dynamic, context-sensitive responses emerging from interactions among environmental exposures, social structures, and lived experience within complex human-environment systems, with cascading effects on motivation, agency, collective action, and disengagement. By embedding affect within socio-environmental systems, the framework explains why similar environmental challenges can generate divergent trajectories of sustained engagement, emotional fatigue, or polarization across populations and over time. Eco-Affective Health distinguishes affective responses to environmental change from psychopathology, reframing them as adaptive signals that reflect the alignment-or misalignment-between sustainability pathways and human experience. The framework's scope, its relationship to cognition, and its position alongside cognate inner-outer sustainability and mindfulness-based frameworks are discussed explicitly, together with directions for future systematic empirical synthesis. By foregrounding affect as a foundational layer of sustainability science, this framework offers a human-centered lens for understanding behavioral persistence, policy legitimacy, and social resilience under accelerating environmental change.
